intro: You eat every day. Breakfast before school. Lunch at a long table. A snack when you get home. Dinner with your family. Every time, someone makes a choice. What goes on the plate? What goes in the cup?

In this unit you learn the five food groups and how they fit on a plate. You learn that water is the everyday drink. You learn that no food is bad, but some foods are for every day and some are for sometimes.
By the end, you will be able to build a plate with parts, count the colors on it, listen to your body when it says hungry and full, share food fairly, and say no thank you the polite way.
bigQuestion: How do you build a plate that helps your body every day?

timeline.t: Breakfast: oatmeal with banana and a cup of milk. Three groups before school.
Lunch: count the colors on your tray. Only one? Add a fruit.
Recess is over. You are hot. Water first, from the fountain.
A new food on the plate. One small taste. Then yes or no thank you.
After school snack: an apple or a cheese stick. Chips wait for the picnic.
Dinner: half the plate is fruits and vegetables. Rice and chicken fill the rest.
Your tummy growls before lunch. That is hungry. Time to eat.
Halfway through dinner you feel done. That is full. Save the rest.
A birthday party. Cake is a sometimes food, and today is sometimes.
Ten crackers, five kids. Two each. Everyone gets some.
A trip to the farm stand. This is where the apples come from.
Plant a bean in a pot on the windowsill. Your own tiny garden.

words.d: a sweet food that grows on a plant, like an apple or a grape
a plant food like a carrot, broccoli or peas
foods like bread, rice and cereal that come from wheat or rice plants
foods like chicken, beans and eggs that help you grow
foods made from milk, like cheese and yogurt
a food you eat most days, like fruit, bread or milk
a food you have now and then, like cake or chips
how your body feels when it has had enough food

test.q: How much of your plate should be fruits and vegetables?
test.why: The rule is half the plate.
Bread comes from wheat. It is a grain.
Yogurt is made from milk, so it is dairy.

test.q: Why eat many colors of fruits and vegetables?
choices: Each color helps your body its own way
test.why: Different colors help different parts of you, like eyes and bones.
Water has no sugar and keeps you cool.

test.q: A new food is on your plate. What do you do?
test.why: One taste is fair. It may take many tries to like it.
Chips are a sometimes food, for a picnic now and then.

test.q: Your tummy feels warm and done. What should you do?
test.why: Full means enough. Listen to your body.

test.q: Nine strawberries, three kids. A fair share is
test.why: Nine split three ways is three each.

test.q: Where does a carrot come from before the store?
test.why: Carrots grow in the ground on farms and in gardens.

write.prompt: Draw and write a lunch plate. Put a food from each of the five groups on it. Add a drink. Then tell why each food is there and which foods on your plate are everyday foods.
tips: Name all five groups: fruit, vegetable, grain, protein, dairy.
Make half the plate fruits and vegetables.
Count the colors. Try for three or more.
Pick water or milk for the drink and say why.

title: Everyday Food and Sometimes Food

chapters.title: The Parts of a Plate
chapters.bigQuestion: What goes on a plate to make a good lunch?

story.title: The Paper Plate Lunch
story.kicker: The class builds a lunch out of colored paper, and the plate tells a story.
paragraphs: Ms. Ortiz put a big paper plate on each table. Next to it was a pile of paper food. Red apples. Green broccoli. Brown bread. A yellow cheese slice. A pink piece of fish.
"Build a lunch," she said. Leo grabbed three pieces of bread and a cookie. Ana picked an apple, some carrots, rice and a chicken leg. She put a paper cup of milk on the side.
Ms. Ortiz walked by. She looked at Leo's plate. "What colors do you see?" Leo looked. "Brown. Just brown." He looked at Ana's plate. Red, orange, white and tan. "Hers looks like a rainbow."
Leo traded one bread for an apple. He traded the cookie for a slice of cheese. Now his plate had four colors. "That is a plate with parts," said Ms. Ortiz. "Every part has a job."
story.think: What did Leo change on his plate, and why do you think it helped?

lessons.title: Fruits and Vegetables
lessons.mainIdea: Fruits and vegetables come from plants and should fill half your plate.
reading: Look at an apple. Look at a carrot. Both grew on a plant. The apple is a *fruit*. The carrot is a *vegetable*. They are two food groups.
Fruits are often sweet. Apples, bananas, grapes and oranges are fruits. Vegetables are things like carrots, broccoli, corn and peas.
Here is the rule. Make half your plate fruits and vegetables. Picture a plate. Draw a line down the middle. One side is plants.

words.d: a sweet food that grows on a plant, like an apple or a grape
a plant food like a carrot, broccoli or peas

look.title: Half a Plate
look.text: Look at a round plate. A line goes down the middle. On the left side there are grapes and green beans. On the right side there is a roll and a piece of chicken. The left side is full. The right side is full too.
look.prompt: Which side of the plate is the fruits and vegetables? Is it half?

check.q: Which food is a fruit?
check.why: A banana is sweet and grows on a plant. It is a fruit.

check.q: How much of your plate should be fruits and vegetables?
check.why: The rule is half your plate. That is a lot of plants.

check.q: Which food is a vegetable?
check.why: Broccoli is a plant food that is not sweet. It is a vegetable.

lessons.title: Grains, Protein and Dairy
lessons.mainIdea: Grains, protein foods and dairy are the other three groups on your plate.
reading: Bread, rice, noodles and cereal are *grains*. Grains come from plants like wheat and rice. They give you energy to run and play.
Chicken, fish, beans, eggs and nuts are *protein* foods. Protein helps your body grow. Milk, cheese and yogurt are *dairy*. Dairy helps your bones.
Count the groups. Fruits. Vegetables. Grains. Protein. Dairy. That is five. A good plate has a little of each one.

words.d: foods like bread, rice and cereal that come from wheat or rice plants
foods like chicken, beans and eggs that help you grow
foods made from milk, like cheese and yogurt

look.title: Sort the Lunch
look.text: Look at a lunch tray. There is a slice of pizza with cheese on top. There is a cup of peaches. There is a carton of milk. There are baby carrots. There is a hard-boiled egg.
look.prompt: Name the group for each food. Which food might fit two groups?

check.q: Which food is a grain?
check.why: Rice comes from a rice plant. It is a grain like bread.

check.q: Which food is dairy?
check.why: Cheese is made from milk. Milk foods are dairy.

check.q: How many food groups are there?
check.why: Fruits, vegetables, grains, protein and dairy make five groups.

lessons.title: Eat a Rainbow
lessons.mainIdea: Different colors of fruits and vegetables help your body in different ways.
reading: Look at a bowl of fruit. Red strawberries. Orange oranges. Yellow bananas. Green grapes. Purple plums. That is a *rainbow* of food.
Each color helps your body a different way. Orange foods help your eyes. Green foods help you grow. So eat many colors, not just one.
Try this at lunch. Count the colors on your plate. One color? Add a fruit. Two colors? Add a vegetable. More colors is better.

words.d: many colors together; a plate with red, green, orange and more

look.title: Colors on Two Plates
look.cite: Example plates from the paper plate lunch story
look.prompt: Which plate has the most colors? What could Leo add to get to three?

check.q: What does eat a rainbow mean?
choices: Eat fruits and vegetables of many colors
check.why: A rainbow of plants means many colors. Each color helps in its own way.

check.q: Your plate has only brown foods. What can you add?
check.why: A fruit or a vegetable adds a new color to the plate.

check.q: Which food helps your eyes?
check.why: Orange foods like carrots help your eyes see well.

lessons.title: Water Every Day
lessons.mainIdea: Water is the everyday drink; it keeps your body working and costs nothing.
reading: You ran at recess. Your face is hot. Your mouth is dry. Your body is asking for *water*. Go to the fountain and drink.
Water is the everyday drink. It has no sugar. It keeps you cool. Milk is a good drink too. It is dairy.
Juice and soda are sweet. They are sometimes drinks. Water is for every day. Keep a water bottle at your desk.

words.d: the everyday drink; it has no sugar and keeps your body cool

look.title: After Recess
look.text: Look at three cups on a table. One has water. One has milk. One has soda. Two kids just ran in from recess. They are hot and thirsty. Each kid gets to pick one cup.
look.prompt: Which cup is the everyday drink? Which one is a sometimes drink?

check.q: Which drink is the everyday drink?
check.why: Water has no sugar and cools your body. It is for every day.

check.q: You are hot after playing. What should you drink first?
check.why: Water cools you and fills up what you lost from sweating.

check.q: Which drink is dairy?
check.why: Milk comes from the dairy group. It helps your bones.

sections.title: New Foods and Where Food Comes From

lessons.title: Trying a New Food
lessons.mainIdea: It can take many tries to like a new food, so take one small taste each time.
reading: A green pepper slice is on your plate. You never ate one. It looks strange. Do you have to like it? No. Do you have to try it? Just a *taste*.
Here is the plan. Take one small bite. Chew. Think. Then say yes or no thank you. Many kids need ten tries to like a new food.
So try again another day. Your tongue can change its mind. Lots of foods you love now were new once.

words.d: one small bite to find out what a food is like

look.title: The Strange Green Slice
look.text: Look at a lunch plate. There is a sandwich, some grapes, and one slice of green pepper. A boy pokes the pepper with his fork. He has never seen one on his plate before. He makes a face.
look.prompt: What is one small thing the boy could do before he says no?

check.q: A new food is on your plate. What should you do?
check.why: One small taste is the fair way to find out if you like it.

check.q: You tried a food once and did not like it. What next?
choices: Eat a whole plate of it
check.why: It can take many tries to like a new food. Your taste can change.

check.q: About how many tries can it take to like a new food?
check.why: Many kids need ten or more tries. Keep tasting.

lessons.title: Farm, Garden, Store
lessons.mainIdea: Food comes from farms and gardens before it gets to the store and your plate.
reading: Look at the apple in your lunch. Where did it come from? The store? Before that, it grew on a tree. The tree was on a *farm*.
A farm grows lots of food. Corn, wheat, apples, beans. Farms also raise cows for milk and chickens for eggs. Trucks take the food to the store.
A *garden* is a tiny farm. You can grow a tomato in a pot. Illinois has many farms. Lots of them grow corn and soybeans.

words.d: a big place where people grow food and raise animals
a small place, even a pot, where you grow food

look.title: The Apple's Trip
look.text: Picture four cards in a row. Card one: an apple tree on a farm. Card two: a truck full of apples. Card three: a store shelf. Card four: an apple in a lunch box. Now the cards get mixed up.
look.prompt: Put the cards back in order. What comes first, and what comes last?

check.q: Where does an apple grow?
choices: On a tree on a farm
check.why: Apples grow on trees. Farms grow them, then stores sell them.

check.q: What comes right after the farm?
check.why: Trucks carry food from farms to stores.

check.q: What is a garden?
choices: A small place to grow food
check.why: A garden is a small farm. Even a pot can be a garden.

review.q: Which two groups should fill half your plate?
review.why: The rule is half your plate fruits and vegetables.

review.q: Which food is a protein food?
review.why: Eggs, beans, chicken and fish are protein foods.
Those five groups make up a plate.

review.q: Why eat many colors of fruits and vegetables?
choices: Each color helps your body a different way
review.why: Orange helps eyes, green helps you grow. Many colors help many ways.
Water has no sugar and is for every day.

review.q: Where does food come from before the store?
review.why: Food grows on farms and in gardens first.

chapters.title: Everyday and Sometimes
chapters.bigQuestion: How do you choose what to eat when there are so many choices?

story.title: Cake and a Bowl of Grapes
story.kicker: At a birthday party, one boy learns there is room for both.
paragraphs: It was Sam's birthday party. On the table sat a big chocolate cake. Next to it was a bowl of grapes and a plate of cheese and crackers. Sam's eyes went straight to the cake.
"Can I have cake now?" he asked. Grandma smiled. "Soon. First, is cake an everyday food or a sometimes food?" Sam thought. "Sometimes. And today is sometimes!"
Grandma laughed. "Yes it is. Have your cake. Have some grapes too, and some water. Then go play." Sam ate one slice of cake. He ate a handful of grapes. He drank a cup of water.
Later, his friend Maya said, "No thank you," when someone gave her a second slice. She was full. Sam noticed. Being full was a real thing. You could feel it.
story.think: Why was cake okay at the party? What else did Sam eat with it?

lessons.title: No Food Is Bad
lessons.mainIdea: No food is bad; some foods are for every day and some are for now and then.
reading: Look at a cookie. Is it bad? No. A cookie is just a cookie. Look at a carrot. Is it good? It is a food. Foods are not good or bad.
Instead we say *everyday* foods and *sometimes* foods. Everyday foods you eat most days. Fruits, vegetables, grains, milk, beans, eggs.
Sometimes foods you have now and then. Cake at a party. Chips at a picnic. Both kinds have a place. The trick is how often.

words.d: a food you eat most days, like fruit, bread or milk
a food you have now and then, like cake or chips

look.title: Two Baskets
look.text: Look at two baskets on a table. One is labeled Every Day. One is labeled Sometimes. In a pile next to them: a banana, a bag of chips, a carton of milk, a lollipop, a bowl of oatmeal, a slice of cake, a carrot.
look.prompt: Sort each food into a basket. Which basket gets more foods?

check.q: Which food is an everyday food?
check.why: Fruit is an everyday food. You can eat it most days.

check.q: Is a cookie a bad food?
choices: No, it is a sometimes food
check.why: No food is bad. A cookie is a sometimes food, for now and then.

check.q: What does a sometimes food mean?
choices: A food you must eat daily
A food you may never eat
A food you have now and then
check.why: Sometimes means now and then, like at a party.

lessons.title: Sweets and Salty Snacks
lessons.mainIdea: Sweets and salty snacks are sometimes foods because they fill you up without helping you grow.
reading: Look at a bag of chips. Salty. Crunchy. Yummy. Look at a candy bar. Sweet. Both are *snacks*. Both are sometimes foods.
Why? Chips and candy fill your belly. But they do not help you grow much. An apple or a cheese stick fills you and helps you.
So save chips for the picnic. Save candy for the party. On a normal day, pick a fruit, a vegetable, or crackers and cheese.

words.d: a small bite of food between meals

look.title: The Snack Shelf
look.text: Look at a kitchen shelf after school. On it: a bowl of apples, a box of cheese sticks in the fridge below, a bag of gummy candy, and a bag of pretzels. A kid is hungry. Dinner is in one hour.
look.prompt: Which snack would you pick for a normal day? Why?

check.q: Which snack is an everyday snack?
check.why: Cheese is dairy. It fills you and helps your bones grow.

check.q: Why are chips a sometimes food?
choices: They fill you but do not help you grow
check.why: Snacks like chips fill your belly without giving your body much to grow with.

check.q: When is a good time for candy?
choices: At a party now and then
check.why: Candy is a sometimes food. A party is a sometimes time.

lessons.title: A Good Breakfast
lessons.mainIdea: Breakfast gives your body fuel so you can think and play all morning.
reading: Picture a morning with no *breakfast*. By ten o'clock your tummy growls. Your head feels foggy. You cannot sit still. Your body ran out of fuel.
Now picture a morning with breakfast. A bowl of oatmeal with banana. Or eggs and toast. Or yogurt and fruit. Your body has what it needs.
Breakfast can be simple. Two or three groups is great. A grain, a fruit, some milk. Even a slice of leftover pizza works.

words.d: the first meal of the day; it gives your body fuel

look.title: Groups in a Breakfast
look.cite: Example breakfasts counted by food group
look.prompt: Which breakfast has the most groups? What could you add to just juice?

check.q: You skip breakfast. What might happen by ten o'clock?
check.why: With no fuel, your tummy growls and it is hard to think.

check.q: Which breakfast has two food groups?
check.why: Toast is a grain and milk is dairy. That is two groups.

check.q: What does breakfast do for you?
choices: Makes you taller in one day
check.why: Food is fuel. Breakfast is the fuel for the morning.

lessons.title: Hungry and Full
lessons.mainIdea: Your body tells you when it is hungry and when it is full, and you can listen.
reading: Your tummy growls. It feels empty. That is *hungry*. Your body is saying, "Time to eat." It is a good sign to listen to.
You eat. After a while your tummy feels warm and done. That is *full*. Your body is saying, "That is enough." Stop and listen.
Eat slowly. Chew. Put your fork down between bites. It takes time for your tummy to tell your brain it is full.

words.d: how your body feels when it needs food; your tummy feels empty
how your body feels when it has had enough food

look.title: Halfway Through Lunch
look.text: Look at a girl at the lunch table. Half her sandwich is gone. Her carrots are gone. Her milk is half gone. She leans back. She yawns a little. Her friend says, "Eat the rest!" She is not sure.
look.prompt: What is her body telling her? What could she do with the rest of her lunch?

check.q: Your tummy growls and feels empty. What is your body saying?
check.why: A growling, empty tummy is the sign of hungry.

check.q: Why eat slowly?
choices: Your tummy needs time to tell your brain it is full
Fast eating is against the law
check.why: It takes time for the full signal to reach your brain.

check.q: You feel full but food is left. What can you do?
choices: Stop and save it for later
check.why: Full means enough. Leftovers can be saved and eaten later.

lessons.title: Sharing Fairly
lessons.mainIdea: When food is shared, everyone gets a fair part before anyone gets more.
reading: Four kids. One plate of eight crackers. How many each? Two. That is a *fair* share. Count the people. Count the food. Split it up.
Do not grab the biggest piece. Do not take a second one before everyone has a first. Ask, "Did everyone get one?"
Fair does not always mean the same. A baby eats less than a big brother. But everyone gets some. Nobody is left out.

words.d: everyone gets a part; nobody is left out

look.title: Sharing Ten Strawberries
look.prompt: Ten strawberries and five kids. How many each? What if two more kids come?

check.q: Eight crackers and four kids. A fair share is how many each?
check.why: Eight split four ways is two each.

check.q: Before you take a second cookie, what do you ask?
check.why: Fair means everyone gets a first share before anyone gets more.

check.q: Which is fair sharing?
choices: Count people and split the food
check.why: Counting people and food is how you make sure nobody is left out.

lessons.title: No Thank You
lessons.mainIdea: You can say no thank you to food politely, and you can tell a grown-up about allergies.
reading: Someone hands you a plate of cookies. You are full. Or you do not want one. What do you say? "No thank you." That is *polite*.
You do not say, "Yuck." You do not make a face. Other people like that food. Just say no thank you and smile.
Some kids cannot eat some foods. Their body gets sick from them. That is an *allergy*. Say so. "No thank you, I have an allergy."

words.d: kind and respectful in what you say and do
when a food makes someone's body sick, so they must not eat it

look.title: The Cookie Plate
look.text: Look at a party table. A grown-up holds out a plate of peanut butter cookies. One kid is full. One kid does not like peanut butter. One kid has a peanut allergy. Each one has to answer.
look.prompt: What should each kid say? Which kid must also tell a grown-up why?

check.q: You do not want a food someone offers. What do you say?
check.why: No thank you is polite. Other people may love that food.

check.q: What is a food allergy?
choices: When a food makes your body sick
check.why: An allergy means a food makes that person sick. They must not eat it.

check.q: A friend has a peanut allergy. What should she do at a party?
choices: Say no thank you and tell a grown-up
check.why: Safety comes first. Grown-ups need to know about allergies.

choices: No, some foods are just for sometimes
review.why: No food is bad. We say everyday and sometimes.
Cake is for parties and now and then.
Food is fuel. Breakfast is the morning's fuel.

review.q: Your tummy feels done and warm. What is it saying?
review.why: Full means enough. Listen and stop.

review.q: Six grapes and three kids. Fair share?
review.why: Six split three ways is two each.

review.q: The polite way to turn down food is to say
review.why: No thank you is kind and respectful.
